#1064. Crystal Palace will sack Pierre Sage after disastrous 16-game spell - this is how his reign fell apart over late, intense sessions, dinner at the training ground and an unpopular assistant manager

Published: 10:17 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 19:16 EST, 9 November 2026

Crystal Palace players and club chiefs have grown frustrated over Pierre Sage's training methods, Daily Mail Sport can reveal - and the 47-year-old will be sacked having won just two of his first ten Premier League matches.

A 3-1 defeat by Liverpool on Sunday saw Palace drop to bottom of the Premier League for the first time in nine years and proved to be the final straw for club bosses, who will tell the Frenchman his time is up.

Daily Mail Sport understands that while the Palace players got on well with Sage, they were frustrated by his late training sessions – with some not starting until 4pm. The regimented routine required players to stay at the training ground for dinner on the night before matches, with some not returning home until 8pm ahead of a 2pm kick-off the following day.

The club's hierarchy, meanwhile, expressed concerns early in the Frenchman's tenure that he was not doing enough defensive work on the training pitch.

Sage's philosophy was that the best way to defend was having the ball, meaning training sessions focused on running, pressing and possession rather than defensive structure.

But the lack of focus led to a poor defensive record, with Palace conceding 30 goals in 16 matches across all competitions. Defending set-pieces and counter-attacks has been a persistent problem for Sage’s side.

Pierre Sage will become the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season after a dismal spell at Crystal Palace

Palace sit rock bottom of the Premier League after winning just two of their first 10 games

Daily Mail Sport understands many players voiced fears they were being pushed too hard in training, with sessions the day before a game particularly intense. There were also significant concerns about the quality of Sage's backroom staff, with his assistant Jamal Alioui proving especially unpopular among the players.

While Palace's on-pitch struggles have been evident, the situation is precarious off the pitch, too. A significant number of staff have resigned amid dissatisfaction with the regime imposed by chief executive Sharon Lacey, with morale understood to be low. Sources have suggested that while Lacey is talented, she struggles to motivate her workforce.

There has also been considerable turnover among senior executives, with six departures over the past 18 months. Chief financial officer Mitesh Velani is set to add to that number in the coming months. One well-placed source told Daily Mail Sport that the disruption to the club’s business operations has the hallmarks of a club heading for relegation.

As Palace look to bail themselves out of trouble, Daily Mail Sport understands former Brentford and Tottenham boss Thomas Frank is in pole position to replace Sage, with six-pointers against Hull City and Coventry City following the international break. Sean Dyche also has admirers at Selhurst Park.

Palace chairman Steve Parish first contemplated sacking Sage over his lack of defensive nous in September, but gave him a stay of execution after Palace kept a clean sheet in a spirited performance away at Leeds on the eve of the international break. However, that display proved an anomaly as Palace shipped 19 goals in the following nine games.

Palace have won just once in their last eight matches in all competitions, beating Fulham 1-0 in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.

In September, Daily Mail Sport revealed tensions had emerged between Sage and Parish when the latter took a dim view of the decision to drop teenage defender Jaydee Canvot in their defeat by Ipswich Town.

Palace paid French club RC Lens £4million in compensation to appoint Sage in June after he won the French Cup, finished second in Ligue 1 behind Paris Saint-Germain and was named manager of the season last term. It was the first time in 10 years that Palace had paid compensation to appoint a manager.

Palace chairman Steve Parish (right) first contemplated dismissing Sage in September over a lack of defensive nous

Palace players found Sage’s training sessions too intense and struggled to adapt to the late schedule

Succeeding Oliver Glasner, Palace's greatest manager, proved too big a task for the 47-year-old.

Following Palace's loss to Liverpool, Sage insisted the Eagles have been playing better than their league position suggests and pleaded for more time.

'A lot of times I’ve said we deserved better and it was the case again (on Sunday),' said Sage. 'My job is not the most important thing, as I always said from the beginning. The most important thing is to find an efficient solution for the team and for the club.

‘I know how important it is for the club to stay in the Premier League. The club just have to believe in (me), and if it's not the case, they will take a decision. I always have confidence in myself because it's a big, big mistake to not be 100 per cent involved in what I have to do.

‘We have to adjust some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions and more efficiency and I think it will be OK.’

#1063. Liverpool face anxious Dominik Szoboszlai wait after knee injury

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Szoboszlai could miss Hungary’s games in the upcoming international break after sustaining the issue in Liverpool’s win over Crystal Palace

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Dominik Szoboszlai could be set to miss the upcoming international break, with the Liverpool star due to undergo tests on his knee as the club face an anxious wait.

The midfielder was withdrawn in the 69th minute of Liverpool’s 3-1 victory at Crystal Palace on Sunday and Hungary have now announced he will have a scan to find out the severity of the issue.

Reds boss Andoni Iraola confirmed after the match that Szoboszlai was “not 100 per cent” after picking up a knee problem, although he set up the opening goal at Selhurst Park, delivering a free-kick for Alexis Mac Allister to convert.

Florian Wirtz scored his first Premier League goal of the season after the interval and Alexander Isak made it three before Eddie Nketiah pulled one back for the bottom-of-the-table hosts with a stoppage-time penalty.

A statement posted by the Hungarian Football Federation on social media read: “(Szoboszlai), who was substituted in the 69th minute of Liverpool’s match yesterday, is undergoing tests following the usual protocol in such cases.

“We will, of course, keep the public informed of developments as soon as possible!”

Iraola could not say what the knee issue would mean for Szoboszlai’s Nations League availability, with Hungary due to face Georgia and Northern Ireland over the next week.

He was equally uncertain about what Liverpool’s medical staff would advise, although admitted “I know what I want”, hinting that he would prefer the 26-year-old not to be involved in the international fixtures.

Speaking after the win at Selhurst Park, Iraola said: “Dom just had, I don’t know (if it was) a problem, but he definitely was not 100 per cent.

“The last thing we need now is to lose players in the international games. Last time, we lost three very important players. It’s the last thing we need, so I hope he can take care of it.

“I think he extended a little bit the knee, he was fine, but not 100 per cent.

“So he has to be careful to see if he can play with the national team or not, but also hope that it doesn’t happen like the other international break when we lost Alex (Alexander Isak), Cody (Gakpo) and Dom, so touch wood we are in a better place in two weeks.”

Iraola said Liverpool will also carry out their own assessments to get a clearer picture of Szoboszlai’s condition.

“I know that he will do everything to go because he loves playing with the national team,” Iraola said. “But he was not 100 per cent now, when he finished the game.

“I suppose they will have to analyse, their medical staff, our medical staff, and see where he is.”

Asked what he believed the Reds medical staff would recommend, Iraola replied: “I know what I want, but I also have to understand the national teams.

“Also, I am sure that if he is fine, he will want to go, but I am not sure if it is going to be fine.”

#1062. Man City look to be crumbling after guilty verdict

Manchester City’s feud with the Premier League following the guilty verdict will dominate their season, but it is now events on the pitch that are proving a genuine concern.

Enzo Maresca has lost three league games in a row and, at the City Ground, there was further evidence of defensive instability, strange team selection and key players underperforming.

Eight games without a clean sheet underlines their vulnerability and Maresca has much to ponder over the international break with his team six points behind leaders Arsenal.

Oliver Glasner has played down the significance of his warning to Nottingham Forest’s squad after their defeat at Brentford has had the desired impact.

The Austrian said last weekend there would be “no compromises” and insisted his players have to fully buy into his philosophy.

Speaking this week, he said: “I didn’t attack anyone directly. We share that we want to be successful and win games. It was not a problem.

“It was much louder outside than I felt it was inside. This is just how I see a relationship has to be. Let’s talk about things if we don’t like things.

“If you never say anything in your relationship with your wife or children, then they will never know. Then I can’t blame somebody because if they don’t know, how can you expect things to change?

“We are now in a society where criticism or the way I talk is negative, but the intention was positive and to change to get better results so that we can all have a better life.”

Gianluigi Donnarumma, who has made three errors leading to goals this season, “recognises that he has made some mistakes,” Enzo Maresca said this week, “but at the same time recognises that he has made some great saves”.

The City manager added: “It is quite easy with him because he recognises any mistake immediately. I’ve spoken to him about it, but I didn’t feel the need to be so deep with him because he already knows and recognises that he has made some mistakes.”

Asked about City players adapting to his philosophy, Maresca said: “I can see my playing style just by working every day with them, but we can still improve many things.

“We know exactly what we are doing well and what we need to improve. It is just a matter of time.”

Elsewhere this afternoon, Martin Odegaard has broken the deadlock at the Emirates to give Arsenal a 1-0 lead over Hull City.

Victory would take Mikel Arteta’s side six points clear of City at the top of the table before this evening’s contest at the City Ground.

Glasner has made two changes to his Forest team following defeat at Brentford last weekend, with Yates and Munoz replacing Ndoye and Aina.

Is this the day the xG gods reward Nottingham Forest? Oliver Glasner’s team sit 19th having won one game all season, but there is no doubt that their performances have been significantly better than results and they might need their luck to turn against Man City team full of firepower.

Despite all of the positive indicators in Forest’s underlying data, Glasner caused some alarm with his comments after last weekend’s defeat at Brentford.

The Austrian said: “We have to accept it’s not good enough. If we lose four of the last five games, it’s not good enough. And that’s why for me, it’s now time that we change things, that I change things, and that’s what I will do.

“I feel now maybe I made too many compromises in some stuff, and it’s always compromises. It’s a clear way. I will tell [the players] what we want to do, what we have to do, and if the players buy in, I think we can have a turnaround, and if not, the sixth manager [since the start of last season] will come in.”

Dangerous words perhaps when you work for Evangelos Marinakis, but John Percy reported this week that Glasner was backed by his players in a squad meeting.

City are smarting from back-to-back defeats by Aston Villa and Brighton, but they created more than enough in both games to claim some sort of result. Nevertheless, there is a persistent sense that their defensive unit remains too marshmellow-like over the course of 38 games, and Forest have the counter-attacking threat to test them.

Glasner has happy memories of playing City, beating them in the 2025 FA Cup final with Crystal Palace, but his Forest reign is in urgent need of a signature victory and performance.

#1061. Alisson reveals future ambitions with Liverpool contract set to expire

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Brazilian goalkeeper, 34, has won every major club honour during his time at Anfield

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Alisson insists he wants to stay at Liverpool beyond the end of his current contract, which is due to expire next summer.

The 34-year-old has won every major club honour since arriving at Anfield in the summer of 2018 following a £67m deal from Roma. In the eight years since, Alisson has developed into one of the best goalkeepers in the world.

Yet the Brazilian’s current deal expires at the end of the current season but, speaking after making several impressive saves in the 3-1 win at Crystal Palace on Sunday, Alisson insists he wants to stay at Liverpool and “at the top level” for a while yet. His agent has begun negotiations with the club about an extension.

Asked if he wants to stay at the club, Alisson replied: “Yes, in my mind. I’m focused on playing every game but in my mind I’m happy to stay. You know, that depends on a lot of aspects and different situations.

“But my will is to stay. I’m happy here, my family is happy here. I’m still hungry for titles and for delivering good performances. I still want to play at the top level for as long as I can. So that’s my thinking on that.”

While Alisson has been the No 1 since joining the club, Giorgi Mamardashvili is a top-tier back-up and the Reds have also signed youngster Lucca Brughmans from Genk for £23.8m. The 18-year-old Belgian will join from the 2027-28 season.

Meanwhile, Alisson was not called up by Brazil boss Carlo Ancelotti for the upcoming friendlies against Japan and Singapore, insisting “we don’t need to test him.” Nonetheless, the keeper acknowledged it was a call taken “against his will.”

He added: “It is beneficial (not going), for sure. You have to use it right because you have a lot of time so if you don’t train, if you don’t prepare, time goes really quick and you need to stay sharp.

“It’s not that I will sit on the couch for a week and then come back training. I still have to work hard but in my mind I can use the time to relax and be more with my family.

“It’s a little bit against my will. What I always want is to be with the national team but I understand this is what I have at the moment and I will use this time and take the benefit from the rest.”

Liverpool head into the international break fourth in the Premier League table, nine points off leaders Arsenal.

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Josh King says Jude Bellingham has taken him “under his wing” in the England camp as the Fulham star hopes to earn a first cap for his country this international break.

The 19-year-old earned a maiden call-up to the England squad on Friday, with Thomas Tuchel hailing the “exciting” player having only just missed out on selection for the first camp of the season across September and October.

It is not King’s first time with the England group, however, with the midfielder picked as part of a five-man development squad for the pre-World Cup training camp in the summer.

It was there that King says Bellingham took on something of a mentorship role for him, crediting the England talisman for helping him integrate.

"There were a lot of people I learned from [in the pre-World Cup camp in Miami],” King said. “Jude was a big person for me. He took me under his wing and tried to make me feel welcome.

"There were a lot of players like that. Harry Kane as well, he was one person who really made me feel welcome and tried to help me through my time there.

"But it's a credit to what England have going here, everyone is a really good person as well as good player on the pitch."

Speaking further on his experience before the World Cup, he said: "It was an amazing opportunity for me. It was nice to meet the lads and get a taste of what it was like to play for England.

“I took a lot of learning from that opportunity. It was a massive part of my journey and it gave me the confidence to start this season well.

"[Tuchel] said to keep going, play well, rack up the minutes. As long as you're trying to perform as well as you can at club level, the rest comes."

King was an injury doubt after suffering groin pain in Fulham’s 1-1 draw with Newcastle on the weekend but his withdrawal was “precautionary”.

"I couldn't turn down the call,” he asserted. “I'm here. I'm all good fitness wise."

King will now hope to make his England debut as Tuchel’s side play their final two Nations League group matches, first hosting Croatia on Thursday before travelling to Madrid to play world champions Spain on Sunday.

Tuchel cited his versatility when explaining why he picked him for the November camp, with King - often a number 10 - able to operate across the midfield as well as up front.

But King isn’t fussy where he plays and is happy to feature wherever Tuchel wants him.

"I'm happy to play anywhere for the manager,” he added. “I have to add other parts to my game, in wider positions you might have to cover defensively or make runs in behind.

"I'm capable of playing lots of different positions, which is probably one of the reasons why I'm here."

#1059. Brown becomes youngest PGA Tour winner in 95 years

Blades Brown also becomes first teenager to win on the PGA Tour since Jordan Spieth in 2013 at 19 years and 171 days old; he came back from a deficit of seven shots with a nine-under 63 to defeat Ben James in the World Wide Technology Championship

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Blades Brown has become the youngest PGA Tour winner since 1931 after the 19-year-old came back from a deficit of seven shots with a nine-under 63 to defeat Ben James in the World Wide Technology Championship.

At 19 years and 171 days old, Brown became the youngest victor since Charles Kocsis won the Michigan Open in 1931 when he was 18, a tournament that was considered a regional event in the early years of the PGA.

James lost a four-shot lead going into the final round at El Cardonal at Diamante and then showed his nerve by smoking a 285-yard shot into 20 feet on the par-five 18th and making eagle to salvage a 70 and force the play-off.

But he missed an eight-foot putt on the second play-off hole as Brown made his three-footer.

"It hasn't set in just yet, I guess, the magnitude of being a PGA Tour winner," Brown said. "Golf is one of the best games, is one of the greatest games in the world. It challenges you mentally, physically, spiritually. It challenges you in every aspect of us, right?

"I just go back to five-year-old Blades that was watching the TV and watching Tiger Woods and all those great players win major championships, and to think that I'm now in a similar spot with having won a PGA Tour event is mind-blowing."

Brown turned pro at 17 and earned his PGA Tour card this year by being among the top 20 in Korn Ferry Tour points.

"I'm so obsessed with this game. It tests you in so many ways," Brown said. "I love golf, all the stuff that goes into it, and I can't wait for what's next."

With eight players separated by two shots on the back nine, Brown ran off three straight birdies to share the lead and then left the mistakes to everyone else.

He hit a superb pitch for birdie on the final hole to post a score of 23-under 265.

That put him one shot ahead of Michael Kim, who played with the Tennessee teen and made birdie from 12 feet for 64 right before Brown made his putt.

Brown now has a two-year exemption, which puts him in the elite Championship Series when the PGA Tour's new model begins in 2028.

The victory also assures Brown of his first major next year at the PGA Championship.

It was another setback for James, who in 13 starts since turning pro has five finishes in the top five, and two runner-up finishes.

The Austin Championship rides into Austin, Texas, bringing PGA Tour excitement to the stunning Omni Barton Creek Fazio Canyons Golf Course.

#1058. Michael Carrick’s future is up to the Man United hierarchy – will they stick or twist?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

United’s recent ramshackle play has left them in the Premier League relegation zone and provided no definitive answer on Carrick’s capability, leaving the club’s decision makers with a big choice

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

As Patrick Dorgu rose highest in a crowded six-yard box to head in a 96th-minute equaliser, Omar Berrada clenched his fists in celebration and Jason Wilcox applauded. Normally, when the cameras pan to them, Manchester United’s chief executive looks on the verge of tears and their sporting director seems to be trying to disappear into zipped-up tops. Not this time. Their joy was probably tinged with relief but perhaps also confusion.

The decision-makers still face another decision. And if the fact Michael Carrick was given extra time to turn their season around may have been because they were paralysed by indecision rather than convinced he represented the solution, Carrick’s last fortnight has not given a definitive answer either way.

His side have not been as spineless and wretched as they were against either Como or Bournemouth. United’s last two matches have brought a victory and a draw. They have also conceded nine in the last three. The faith Wilcox, Berrada – and, by extension, Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers – showed in Carrick has been rewarded in parts of the games against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa, but certainly not over the full 90 minutes of any. Sunday’s 4-4 draw against Villa, following Tuesday’s 3-2 win over Roma, seemed to underline that United are not a serious football team any more. Indeed, ragged and ramshackle, there are times when they are barely a team at all.

And yet, with Carrick imperilled, they have summoned something from within, twice in five days. Maybe they are playing to save the manager’s skin.

But the precedents also included United’s previous 4-4 draw, 11 months ago against Bournemouth and in the final weeks of Ruben Amorim’s reign. Were they playing for him, or just in a game that took on a life of its own? There was also the example of Amorim’s 5-4 win over Lyon; like Carrick’s triumph over Roma, the craziness of it was scarcely a blueprint for future success.

So Wilcox and Berrada have much to ponder. When they opted not to sack Carrick two weeks ago, perhaps it was a case of timing, that their succession planning was not sufficiently advanced to move. They may have been put off by the Fletcher precedent: United’s former players tended to have excellent records as caretaker managers until Darren Fletcher found it tougher in January. Wilcox and Berrada might have found themselves without an ideal interim or permanent replacement.

Now an international break provides the chance to make a change. The onus switches to United’s powerbrokers, even if they again opt not to act. Carrick has confirmed he will not quit. “That’s not going to happen,” he said. Sacking him could make unpopular figures even more unpopular; or it could save the crowd from turning on an Old Trafford favourite. In the triangle of players, manager and hierarchy, only Carrick has had the vocal backing of the Stretford End of late. Carrick may have credit in the bank with the money men as well: by transforming last season and taking United into the Champions League, he made the club £100m.

But he has also taken them into the relegation zone in November. In itself, that could be deemed a sackable offence. Indeed, United have made their worst start in 40 years, when they also took eight points from their first 10 games, when they sacked their manager in November. But Ron Atkinson left them one place above the bottom three; they dropped into it after Sir Alex Ferguson’s first game, a 2-0 defeat at Oxford.

United even had more league wins at this stage in 1973-74, in the season when they went on to be relegated, when, at Christmas, their joint top scorer was the goalkeeper, Alex Stepney.

And for now, United are in danger of the drop. When Amorim talked of them being in a relegation battle in December 2024, they were not really; they had enough of a cushion. Not now; while December could offer some respite, containing meetings with the rest of the current bottom five, the risk is that United’s plight worsens before then.

There is no quick fix, no easy answers. Maybe United’s dismal defence will have more solidity when Luke Shaw is finally fit again. There was certainly the sense that the returning players could prove to be reinforcements. The fit-again Dorgu, who scored in Carrick’s first two games in January, might have scored in his last or extended his tenure. There are signs that, after so many were out of form, a couple of Carrick’s squad are belatedly showing something resembling their best, as Matheus Cunha has in the last two matches. But there are others who have got still worse.

So United need someone to transform their season in the way Carrick himself did last year, even if it is only the temporary boost a new-manager bounce can provide. But they can’t sack Michael Carrick and then appoint Michael Carrick. Do Wilcox and Berrada stick or twist? If the outside world does not know, perhaps they don’t either.

#1057. These AI agents design your perfect robot-powered lab — and run it for you

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Artificial-intelligence agents can devise a detailed procedure for a robotic arm and test it in a virtual laboratory.Credit: Jiaru Bai & Yuchi Zhao, University of Toronto

Laboratory robots are tireless and uncomplaining, but they have narrow skill sets, limited mobility and an inability to get out of each other’s way. Now, a system of artificial-intelligence agents promises to help lab robots do their best work.

In this process, a scientist describes their research programme and lab set-up to the agents, which then create step-by-step experimental protocols for the lab’s robots. The agents also generate a virtual version of the lab and test the protocols there. They can then direct the robots in the real lab to perform the research.

Robot chemist sparks row with claim it created new materials

Robot chemist sparks row with claim it created new materials

The agents can even design an entire lab from scratch, using a virtual one to work out the ideal placement for instruments and robots.

The system is described in a preprint posted in October to arXiv1. It has not been peer reviewed.

In a test, the agents wrote more than 200 commands directing a robotic arm to move between and interact with instruments in an existing lab space. The agent simulated the steps in the virtual lab to ensure that it all worked smoothly, then directed the real-life arm to carry out procedures to measure the optical properties of nanocrystals.

The concept is “very cool” and could drastically reduce the effort required to set up automated labs, says Evan Collins, a bioengineer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. But integrating the cameras and sensors that the agents need to direct experiments effectively could require more resources than does setting up a lab manually, he says.

The simulations would make it easy to plan robotic movements that avoid collisions between robots and other objects in the lab, says Collins.

This could ease the process of getting labs up and running, given that setting up an automated lab is often a time-consuming process of trial and error followed by extensive testing and troubleshooting. Because the agents conduct all the planning and testing in a simulated environment, there is no need for researchers to “babysit the system” after it’s built, says Yuchi (Allan) Zhao, a roboticist at the University of Toronto in Canada and co-author of the preprint.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03587-x

Bai, J. et al. Preprint at arXiv https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.23826 (2026).

#1056. Michael Carrick is ‘clear’ about his plans as he clings onto Man Utd job

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

United go into the international break in the Premier League relegation zone after the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Michael Carrick remains confident in his ability to oversee Manchester United’s resurgence after a “right mixed” three weeks left his team in the relegation zone and the head coach’s future under scrutiny.

The 20-time league champions will spend the November international break in 18th place as their wait to add to August’s solitary Premier League win against Ipswich continued against Aston Villa.

United showed spirit and all too familiar flaws as Sunday’s helter-skelter clash ended in a 4-4 draw after substitutes Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu scored in stoppage time following Tuesday’s 3-2 comeback win against Roma.

Carrick insisted afterwards that he would not walk away from a job that looked like it could be taken from him a fortnight ago and the international break provides an opportunity for the club to take stock.

Asked if the two-week pause comes at a good time for the group, the under-fire United boss said: “Yeah, it’s been a right mixed week or two or three, really, if you’re looking at the events.

“But I’m pretty clear where we need to go and how we need to get there.

“Obviously some of the boys will be flying off around the world and different things, and the group will be split for 10 days or so.

“But as a normal international week is, you know, we’ll have some training. We’ll have one or two days off, but not too much. But we’ll train, and we’ll get ready for the next game.”

The final international break of the year would be a logical time for United to make a change given there is no free midweek until mid-December after returning with a trip to rivals Liverpool on November 22.

But Carrick is steadfast in his belief that he can lead the embattled side up the standings having seen enough positives since a 4-1 defeat at Como and 3-0 home loss to Bournemouth left his job hanging by a thread.

United failed to take their chances and saw Lisandro Martinez sent off in a 2-0 loss at Chelsea, before Tuesday’s stirring 3-2 Champions League comeback against Roma was followed by the dramatic Villa draw.

“Goals change games, and you’ve got to deal with it, and it’s part of something we have to improve on drastically,” Carrick said.

“But there’s more than enough. We’re just making it too difficult for ourselves at the moment in certain times.”

Carrick is far from perfect but has been let down by United’s transfer business in the view of outspoken defender Martinez and the fans who frequently aim chants at director of football Jason Wilcox.

Left-back was among the areas of need and Luke Shaw’s injury has seen Diogo Dalot often deployed there, but frustrations with the United full-back reached boiling point on Sunday as supporters cheered his substitution.

Head coach Carrick, who was unaware of United’s full-back then being hounded as he left the ground, said: “We’ve got to be careful with that, I think.

“I understand the frustration. I understand the disappointment of the supporters, so I get it. We’re all frustrated. We’re all disappointed.

“The players are as much as anyone, I guarantee you that. Diogo gives absolutely everything. He’s played in different positions. He’s played left-back. He’s played really well at times.

“He gives a penalty away. He knows that, maybe he can do a little bit better. Alright, that’s part of it, he’s made a mistake.

“But he cares an awful lot, and he’s given everything, so I like what he brings to the team. I like what he brings to the group.”

#1055. Liverpool’s expensive attack feast on Palace to leave Sage looking doomed

Crystal Palace are playing this season as if afflicted by a curse. They seem to have made a terrible deal, possibly involving a monkey’s paw. As a result, Pierre Sage’s team were able to defend credibly for around 44 minutes of each half, on one condition: They must switch off completely, at least twice per game.

This being the Premier League, those lapses in concentration are usually punished. A mostly compact performance out of possession briefly became as porous as a bath sponge when Liverpool eased into a 2-0 lead, nine minutes after half-time. Florian Wirtz did not even need to finish cleanly to score his first Premier League goal of the season, striding on to an unopposed low cross from Bradley Barcola and killing the match as a contest.

Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz combine to put Liverpool 2-0 up! 🔴 https://t.co/F6sw33FkYZ

Major signings need to lay down a marker when arriving at Liverpool. Barcola has his hat-trick at LASK in the Champions League, but we are still waiting for a stirring big-match-defining contribution from him since his summer arrival. Arguably the same could be said for Wirtz, nearly 18 months since he joined.

Neither left Selhurst Park looking like the world-beaters they did occasionally for their previous clubs. Still, one misfiring attacker creating a goal for another represents progress and all great partnerships must start somewhere. Lennon and McCartney would improve after 1958’s Too Bad About Sorrows.

If there was ever a place for the least-productive expensively assembled attacking group in the league to find form it was surely south London on this Sunday lunchtime. Liverpool came in with two defeats in their previous two but, European trophy aside, it has been a lousy 2026 for Palace.

They have the most defeats of any ever-present Premier League team and began (and ended) the weekend with the worst defensive record. They have conceded twice as many goals from headers as any other team. Even their most loyal fan group has disbanded.

Alexis Mac Allister opened the scoring in gut-punching fashion, after a series of Palace near-misses. Chairman Steve Parish rubbed his face in the directors’ box, in the style of peak-stress era Guardiola. None of this looked good for Sage, who appears on the brink of dismissal, with Thomas Frank his most likely replacement.

Asked if he expected to remain in his job on the other side of the international break Sage said he deemed his prospects “better than you, I think”.

“We deserved better today,” the Frenchman said. “But football is not about what you deserve it is about how efficient you are and today we had a lack of efficiency”.

Counter-intuitively, it was Palace’s flashes of promise which suggested the Frenchman might be doomed. There is enough to work with here, and plenty going marginally against Palace to suggest a change in leadership might prompt a turnaround, however unfair it would be on their manager. Yéremy Pino hit the bar, Jorgen Strand Larsen had his composed close-range goal struck from the record by VAR, Daichi Kamada stung Alisson Becker’s palms and the Brazilian saved well again from Adam Wharton’s feathered header.

The other factor which seems likely to condemn Sage is his team’s boneheaded defensive lapses. Liverpool were awarded a debatable free-kick out wide, Quinten Timber let Mac Allister run off him too easily and he duly nodded Dominik Szoboszlai’s delivery past Dean Henderson with ease. Another header conceded.

Liverpool have taken the lead against Crystal Palace thanks to Alexis Mac Alister's header! 💥 https://t.co/kNal7qsQ35

Mac Allister, formerly of Brighton, endeared himself to the Holmesdale Road Stand with a priggish celebration. There was some blowback from the seats closest, but a more dominant sense of resignation. Someone in the adjoining block took out their phone and snapped a picture. Formerly hated rival scoring against you, rubbing it in with his celebration: truly one to show the grandkids.

Liverpool had put together little of substance until then, with Wirtz drifting through another half, Alexander Isak looking keen but flawed and Barcola spooning a promising shot into low-Earth orbit. Isak had his moment in the end, checking back to finish calmly at the end of a counter-attack against a tiring defence. Eight for the season for him and an assist for Wirtz, too, although it was hardly a pass of Molbyesque majesty.

“Happy for him,” Iraola said of Wirtz, also praising Isak’s movement for the German’s goal. “I think [Wirtz] has been very unlucky in the Premier League, a couple of goals disallowed and situations where he deserves honestly to score.”

He may not have reached Eddie Nketiah’s stoppage-time penalty, but made a series of brave saves and deserved a clean sheet. For all that attacking talent, the long-serving goalkeeper still looks like one of Iraola’s most important players.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Crystal Palace and Liverpool at Selhurst Park.

The pressure is building on Palace head coach Pierre Sage, who desperately needs a win to lift the mood and propel the club out of the relegation zone. Nottingham Forest’s impressive 3-1 win over Manchester City on Saturday evening means that Palace have dropped to a lowly 19th and are two points from safety. To make matters worse, Sage’s beleaguered side have also conceded the most goals in the division (21 in nine games).

On Thursday night, Daichi Kamada’s stoppage-time equaliser rescued a 1-1 home draw in the Europa League against Hoffenheim, after Palace delivered an alarmingly lacklustre performance.

Meanwhile, Liverpool also endured midweek European torment, as Andoni Iraola’s men fell to an error-ridden 3-2 defeat away at Fenerbahce in the Champions League, having previously lost 1-0 to Arsenal in their most recent Premier League encounter on Merseyside last weekend, which has left the club in sixth but just five points behind second-place Man City.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Iraola said: “I think that’s the challenge, especially in a club like Liverpool. One week ago in this same press conference, we were on a run, everything was in a good place and we were in a better mood. And now, two defeats, it changes. It has to change and it has to be like this in a club like ours. Now we have to react after two defeats.”

As for Palace’s team news, Jean-Philippe Mateta is serving the first match of a three-game domestic ban after he was sent off for Palace in the 2-0 defeat to Tottenham last time out in the league. Liverpool’s long-term absentees include Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Jeremie Frimpong, while Ryan Gravenberch could also miss out after struggling with a heel injury.

#1054. Thomas Tuchel clarifies Jordan Pickford's England role amid No 1 uncertainty

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Tuchel had suggested Pickford may split game time with understudy James Trafford

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Thomas Tuchel has confirmed Jordan Pickford remains England’s number one but suggested he may again split game time with understudy James Trafford this week.

The Everton goalkeeper has been one of the first names on the team sheet ever since Sir Gareth Southgate made him first choice heading into the 2018 World Cup in Russia.

Pickford has played a key role in every tournament since but found himself in the unusual position of watching from bench at the start of England’s first meet-up since the World Cup.

The 93-cap keeper only played in half of the four-game autumn camp as Tuchel decided to start up-and-coming Leeds player Trafford in the first two fixtures.

Asked if Pickford was no longer number one, Tuchel said: “No, he is. But nothing has changed. The competition is on there as well, like for the outfield players.

“Traff gets regular starts now, that’s what we wanted. James Trafford did well. They shared the matches last time.

“I’m not sure what we will do. There’s an opportunity that we maybe do this again.

“I have to speak with our goalkeeper coach. But the goalkeepers, they are a bit of a unit for themselves, and rightly so.”

Tuchel has two more Nations League matches to round off a hectic year, with Thursday’s Wembley clash against Croatia followed by a trip to World Cup winners Spain on Sunday.

“It’s slightly different (to outfield players), but when do I have a chance to see another goalkeeper, if not in Nations League? If not in high-pressure matches?” the head coach asked.

“So, we had James against Spain, we asked ourselves, ‘Is this fair for James Trafford to straightaway go against Spain?’.

“But I think it’s exactly what we need because what happens if Jordan Pickford is injured? What happens if he’s not available?

“So, it’s better to test it. Jordan knows about this. That we want to use Nations League for exactly that.

“But at the moment, nothing has changed. At the moment, he’s the number one and he just feels a bit of competition, which is good for him.”

Not only is it pushing Pickford but, Tuchel says, has shown the 32-year-old’s quality of character.

“I was very impressed and a bit surprised by his reaction when we spoke to him,” the England boss added.

“I thought he’d be less of a fan than he proved to be because he said he totally understands it.

“He impressed me a lot last time. We spoke to him, it was a very short conversation. It was very positive.

“He said, ‘Yeah, let’s do this, Traff deserves it and I will push him’. And he didn’t change at all.

“If he changed, he changed even to the positive, he pushed Traff, he gave him a good feeling. So very impressive, he did it very well.”

#1053. Chelsea bullied by Brian Brobbey and Sunderland

Talk about cramming everything in. Brian Brobbey only played for 67 minutes but, in that time, he collected a yellow card, ripped Levi Colwill’s shirt and earned himself a standing ovation after morphing into a battering ram.

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, said there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored. Everyone, that is, bar Xabi Alonso.

“No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle. “He’s stoppable – but only when you defend better than we did. We were not bullied. We didn’t produce enough.”

That is one way of putting it. Another would be to say Brobbey was everything that Chelsea, much to Alonso’s disgust, were not: a bristling menace, a steamroller wearing a pair of boots, a player on a mission to help transform the mood – Enzo Le Fée’s decisive spot kick owed everything to Brobbey.

Chelsea arrived on Wearside looking to establish themselves in the top four ahead of the break but, instead, Alonso watched through his fingers as Sunderland reminded everyone why they were the joyous story of last season, a beautiful mix of inspiration and perspiration.

In fairness to the Chelsea manager, he refused to get caught in the minutiae of contentious penalty decisions – one that Chelsea were denied, another that they conceded – and could only lament as Sunderland ground out their first Premier League win since August 30, 70 long days ago.

“It wasn’t the best game,” Alonso said. “I think that we didn’t deserve more than probably one point, maybe. We need to be more consistent on the move, to get the ball from one side to the other, and we didn’t do that good enough. We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win.”

Unlike Sunderland. If you had turned up at the Stadium of Light without looking at the Premier League table, you would not have believed the hosts were bottom and you would not have given credence to the idea Le Bris, who has worked miracles these past two years, was under pressure.

Things, however, could not have started worse for Le Bris. Though Granit Xhaka has not shown last season’s form in these challenging opening months, the game plan was built around him, so to see the Sunderland captain hobbling off after three minutes was symptomatic of how things have gone for the Wearsiders.

“He felt something in the final sprint of the warm-up,” Le Bris explained. “We don’t know how bad it is.”

He is not the kind of coach, though, who will bemoan bad fortune. Le Bris sent on Jules Ahoka to replace Xhaka and watched as he, along with colleagues in red and white, set about trampling all over Chelsea’s intentions with incessant hard work.

Yet there was more to it. Sunderland can play, either intricately or directly, and a lovely move in the 12th minute needed a desperate, sliding intervention from Pep Chavarría’s to stop Trai Hume’s volley sliding in at the far post.

In the next attack, another Chemsdine Talbi cross – the Moroccan having been found by a peach of a pass from goalkeeper Robin Roefs – invited Brobbey to inflict maximum damage, but the Dutchman made a hash of his opportunity.

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The momentum could have changed completely in the 23rd minute. Alonso, his players and staff were convinced they would be given a penalty after Cole Palmer tumbled when his legs tangled with Luke O’Nien but, after a lengthy delay, VAR Nick Hopton felt there was no case to answer.

Hopton was involved again in the 33rd minute but, as Alonso said, Chelsea only had themselves to blame. Colwill simply could not contain Brobbey when he began marauding, grappling, grabbing and clipping the Dutchman’s heels. Le Fée did the rest, sending Mike Penders the wrong way.

Enzo Le Fee dispatches the penalty as Sunderland take the lead against Chelsea! 🔴⚪️ https://t.co/cCtYsHVWB9

From that point, Chelsea were in trouble, no matter how many changes Alonso made. They huffed, puffed, but nothing worked. They had come up against a red-and-white wall, fortified by constant backing from the stands, and the west Londoners were never going to knock it down.

One incident, as the clock ticked towards 90 minutes, encapsulated everything good about this Sunderland display when O’Nien chased down substitute Geovany Quenda to make a challenge. Another moment of defending from Thomas Meunier on Morgan Rogers was exceptional.

“You could see our identity and our togetherness and the way we managed the game,” said Le Bris, who was booked when hectoring referee Jarred Gillett. “These three points were critical. It was a struggle at times to manage situations. We showed as a group real heart.”

And nobody did that more than Brobbey. No wonder Le Bris will be hoping Xavi Hernández, the Netherlands head coach, handles him with care over the next 10 days. On this form, he will be the fuel that drives Sunderland’s quest for survival.

“You know when you come here in this stadium it will be a difficult game and that was the matter tonight. We knew it would be tough, we are disappointed we lost the game. At one point it went very fast from side to side. Sometimes we had to control. With 11 behind the ball it is difficult to find the spaces.”

On where Chelsea stand ahead of the international break...

“How you do – good or not – it is a matter of staying together. The international break is coming so the lads can be calm in the head and when we all come back we need to be motivated to go again.”

“For me it wasn’t a penalty. He barely touched him, I think it was the other way round. He grabbed him.”

The replay suggests he may well have been hard done by but VAR also is having nothing of it...it was a foul as none of the marauding Sunderland players, O’Nien among them (obviously), got the ball and most definitely got Palmer...think the hosts got away with that one.

Yellow card for Ahoka for a foul on Caicado, he may need to walk a tightrope for the rest of the match. But it’s an illustration of the energy and purpose with which Sunderland have approached this match.

Sunderland have looked the better side so far and have had the better chances.

Better from Chelsea in the sense that they controlled the game for two minutes. Lots of good, neat passing but no end product, it’s all in front of a composed Sunderland defence.

Another good chance for Sunderland and once again Talbi proves his worth. He cuts back onto his right and delivers a peach of a cross from the left. Brobbey gets in front of his man and all he has to do is hit the target...alas his first-time shot goes wide. That should be 1-0 to the hosts who are the better side at the moment.

Good from Sunderland who look so much more energetic than at any point during their previous few matches. Ahoka does well in the middle before freeing Talbi down the left. The Moroccan gets in a cross and Le Fee’s shot is blocked. Promising signs for the hosts.

What a blow this is for Regis Le Bris. Less than two minutes gone and Granit Xhaka is having to leave the pitch with an obvious injury. Some fans around the press box booed Xhaka as he was hobbling off - is that a hangover from his attempts to move to Chelsea? - but on afternoon when Le Bris needed everything to go his way, he’s already on the back foot.

Neto is in the Sunderland half but three Sunderland players snap at his heels like a hyperactive dog after a bone. Chelsea haven’t been allowed to settle yet. Plenty of time to go though...

Sunderland are looking to find Brobbey at every opportunity, but Chelsea’s backline intercept well. Nothing of note created so far, but the hosts are on the front foot, which is what they and the fans needed.

Sunderland attack down the right with Meunier, nothing comes of it but the hosts look as though they mean business here. A minute later Sadiki and Brobbey nearly combine to create something. Close but no cigar...

Bad news for Sunderland, Xhaka is down and it looks as though he may well have to come off...oh dear. While he’s not been at his best this season he’s still the man the side looks towards for inspiration (an boy do they need that is dollops today...)...and, indeed he is forced off. Ahoka, who is highly rated but raw replaces him. The Congolese player now has a big chance to make a name for himself.

Chelsea with the early possession, but they go backwards and the hosts are up and at them with the press and the visitors have to go back to Penders in goal.

They’re under way at the Stadium of Light, Sunderland are in their famous red and white and Chelsea in their away outfit of black shirts and shorts and yelow socks.

As the Stadium of Light remembers all those who lost their lives in war.

The Last Post is played and the minute’s silence is impeccably observed.

Warming-up in our Remembrance shirt ❤️ https://t.co/aTB8sfdLKP

And we’re moments away from kick-off in the North East.

This is a big afternoon for both teams. It will be an emotional one, too, for Jordan Henderson, who started his career at Sunderland many years ago. Xabi Alonso has confirmed he has been picked because of the quality he provides, rather than any sentimental value, and Regis Le Bris revealed ahead of the fixture he tried to bring the England international home during the summer window, when Chelsea attempted to sign Granit Xhaka.

“Jordan is a great player, first of all,” said Le Bris. “For the connection with the club, it’s not my part. It was with Flo [Ghisolfi, director of football] and Kyril [Louis-Dreyfus, the Sunderland owner], they had conversations.

Has just said that Sunderland, and in particular Brian Brobbey, can ‘get at’ the Chelsea defence of Palestra, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria. I am not sure he has seen much of the Sunderland attack this year, but Brobbey is a handful for any defence.

“We have to stay consistent and true to our identity. It’s always difficult to predict what the other side does but you have to focus on yourself and connect with the fans and impose our ideas.”

On whether they can get a result today...

“I hope so... I see the players every day, they care and sometime its hard to understand the unforced errors.”

“He’s loved by fans and team, so we know the situation at beginning of season. He is an important player for us and didn’t start for various reasons, but has qualities run in behind and finish - he’s excited worked and has worked hard.”

I mentioned earlier that Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season. But the manner of the victories revealed more than the scorelines. In both matches, especially the second, the west Londoners looked somewhat lightweight and easily bullied.

This season Xabi Alonso has been determined to ensure that that is not the case this season.

In the land of the Premier League giants, Chelsea have been on the small side in recent seasons. But they are no longer being looked down upon and are finally showing signs of being capable of going toe-to-toe physically with opponents.

Sunday’s opponents Sunderland ran Chelsea off the park twice last season. Only once, in the 36th Premier League game of the campaign against Liverpool, did Chelsea cover more distance than their opposition.

For Sunderland that argument is easy to make – they are bottom of the Premier League, are without a win since August and for morale, if nothing else need at least a point, though three is really what the doctor orders.

For Chelsea – fourth in the table and with three wins in their past four league outings – the argument that this is a must-win game is harder to make, but bear with me here...

Facing a Sunderland team who are suffering from the worst of both worlds – blunt in attack and pitiful in defence (what a difference from last season...) and have proven all too easy to beat (as their 2-0 home defeat Zagreb illustrated on Thursday) – the west Londoners are expected to win. Fail to return to the capital with the three points and there will once again be question marks over Xabi Alonso’s side. They are flaky and flashy in equal measure, able to play and win well in spurts, but once again unable to mount sustained pressure needed for a title challenge and forced to battle it out for the hope of a top-four spot at best. The hosts doubtless wish that their ‘issues’ were as golden as today’s opposition. For Trai Hume, who scored in this fixture last season, the Sunderland players are at fault for the sorry start to the season and he wants to put right the wrongs so far, starting today.

“I couldn’t tell you what’s changed. “We’re still together as a club, as a team. I think the run of form we’re on, it would be easy to think we’re not, but we are. We are really upset with how we’ve been playing, and the results don’t lie. We haven’t been good enough and we know that. We have to address that.”

#1052. Los Angeles Golf Club make history by winning inaugural WTGL match

The inaugural WTGL season teed off at SoFi Center in Florida with Los Angeles Golf Club defeating New York Golf Club; the opener included walk-up videos from the parking lot, flashy intros for the fans on hand, some funky fashion and Serena Williams in attendance

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Los Angeles Golf Club sealed a 3-1 victory over New York in an historic first WTGL match at SoFi Center.

Lydia Ko and Michelle Wie West were among the six players in action who treated an audience of 1,500 fans at the indoor venue in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida to some spectacular shot-making, several dramatic near-misses and pure entertainment between the mic'd-up players.

Wie West, Alison Lee and Gaby Lopez eventually out-duelled Rose Zhang and her team-mates in Linn Grant and Ko.

New York's Zhang broke new ground as she hit the first tee shot, one that she blasted 301 yards into the fairway on Cut The Sails.

Wie West came agonisingly close to registering a hole-in-in-one at the par-three seventh as Los Angeles built a narrow 2-1 lead over New York after the first nine holes of team play. New York took number 5, and Lee took down Grant on number 11

In the closing holes, New York had chances, but Zhang missed two short putts on the 13th hole and Grant missed a 10-foot putt on the 14th.

That secured the win for Los Angeles, 3-1, before the teams tied the final hole.

"Our purses are growing up, and we get to play the most amazing golf courses we've ever played," Lee said. "For people to experience and see us play in a different setting, in a more intimate and personal setting, is very different, and hopefully it can bring more eyeballs to the game."

Los Angeles will have a chance to build a verifiable winning streak on Tuesday as the inaugural season begins to ramp up.

Wie West and co will take on Motor City Golf Club, who boast a line-up led by Lexi Thompson and Brooke Henderson.

The WTGL follows on from the success of the Tomorrow's Golf League (TGL), founded by Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy's TMRW Sports, in partnership with the PGA Tour.

The women's edition of the tech-infused golf league will see LPGA Tour stars feature in a unique team format, with five teams (representing five different cities) of five-player rosters confirmed for the inaugural season.

The season-long competition takes place across November and December at the SoFi Center in Florida, a purpose-built indoor venue, with every shot live and all the players mic'd up for the made-for-TV format.

Both the 2026 and 2027 editions of WTGL will be broadcast exclusively on Sky Sports as part of an expansion of its golf rights, which also includes a further two years of TGL presented by SoFi.

Every match will be exclusively live on Sky Sports Golf, Sky Sports+ or Sky Sports Mix, while repeats will be available the following day on Sky Sports Golf. You can also download the Sky Sports App for news, highlights, scores and reports.

#1051. The real reason why Man United are desperate to avoid sacking Michael Carrick

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

United’s dramatic comeback against Aston Villa raises more questions around the direction of the club, explains Miguel Delaney, with Carrick’s demise exposing a more worrying truth about the club

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

If there were times when Manchester United’s 4-4 draw with Aston Villa tested credulity, the outcome has gone beyond that.

It is remarkable that the Premier League’s most successful ever club are in the relegation zone, over a quarter of the way into the season, as late as the November international break... and there is still no action regarding the manager’s position.

The entire lack of response feels in-keeping with a general passivity that has allowed historically bad results to become normalised.

It should be stressed that making this point is not a push to sack Michael Carrick. It’s just a reflection on a remarkable turn of events.

As one experienced football figure with a lot of knowledge of United put it, “it’s just insane”.

Not everyone thinks like that. One source at a rival club told the Independent during the game on Sunday that sacking Carrick would not really change much.

And that probably touches on a reason why what looks like mere place-holding can endure.

The United hierarchy can tell themselves that the first-half performance offers enough to keep Carrick in a job, especially with the way they ultimately rallied to claim a point.

It is probably true that his team could have been out of sight at half-time, as could have been the case at Chelsea.

All of that was nevertheless surrounded by problems that look endemic, especially how they were so easily opened at the beginning of both halves and just seemed beaten once Villa got a second two-goal lead.

Even describing "a second two-goal lead" seems absurd, and the latter comeback still had a freakish nature. It didn’t come from an impressively concerted team pressure in the way that the first comeback occurred. It came out of nothing but at once seemed dependent on Villa’s substantial complex about playing at Old Trafford.

And it’s still just a point, that leaves United 19th and without a Premier League win since August.

Little wonder the players looked beaten afterwards.

They’re aware of more fundamental problems, that many will say they themselves represent.

To try to address that would also raise a bigger issue for the hierarchy.

Not what to do with Carrick but what next.

As was said on these pages and in the Inside Football newsletter last week, no one is actually making the decision on the manager, but they also don’t know who to look to.

There are caveats and reservations about every potential candidate.

The obvious name that Sir Alex Ferguson represented 40 years ago just isn’t there.

It’s not even like six or eight years ago, when Mauricio Pochettino seemed set for the job. His name has subsequently been broached again, but there’s obviously a question of whether he is the same manager.

No candidate is currently forcing the call.

The comeback against Villa, consequently, wasn’t just a badly needed reprieve for the team. It was a reprieve for the hierarchy. They are seemingly spared a decision.

They can continue to indulge the thinking that this might just correct itself, even if that feels as much of a Hail Mary as Patrick Dorgu’s late push or Senne Lammens somewhat controversially going up for that corner.

That is arguably how you turn a situation that is embarrassing into one that has real concerns; where you might not just temporarily find yourself in the relegation zone but actually face a battle.

It’s almost to indulge in magical thinking, rather than addressing the core problems at hand.

But, of course, if United do have to make a decision on yet another manager, it is at the point now when much more of the focus is on those making the decision.

This is at least the fourth time that the Sir Jim Ratcliffe leadership have been in this position, but it’s probably more than that given all of the three coaches they have worked over have had absurdly extended stays of execution.

They should have sacked Erik ten Hag in summer 2024 only to prevaricate and end up doing it a mere four months later.

Ruben Amorim tested their stance for almost as long.

And, now, Carrick’s tenure has tested the very standards of the club.

There have been so many records and previous nadirs just plummeted through. The team apparently can get worse.

And then you have one of the reasons for that, that goes way beyond Carrick: all of him, Ten Hag and Amorim are very different managers.

So are pretty much all of the potential candidates.

This does not look like best-in-class practice.

Instead, this is Manchester United right now.

It’s become a club where the previously unthinkable has become a new normal.

#1049. Aberdeen sack Robinson

Aberdeen have parted ways with Robinson after their 4-0 loss to Hibernian; the Dons are second-bottom after just three wins from 12 Premiership games this season; the 51-year-old left St Mirren to take charge at Pittodrie in March; Stuart Duff placed in interim charge

Football Journalist @AlisonGConroy

Aberdeen have sacked Stephen Robinson with the club sitting 11th in the Scottish Premiership.

It follows their 4-0 defeat to Hibernian on Saturday, which came just a week after the Pittodrie club lost their League Cup semi-final to Rangers.

The Dons have lost seven of their 12 Premiership matches this season, including four of their last five.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Fans inside Pittodrie called for his sacking during their defeat to Hibs, with the 51-year-old admitting the performance was not good enough, and ultimately bringing to an end his eight-month stint at the club.

Robinson joined from Scottish Premiership rivals St Mirren in March, signing a deal until the summer of 2029.

He arrived having led the Buddies to three consecutive top-six finishes, plus won the League Cup trophy in December. While he did save the club from the relegation play-offs last season, this season has seen not gone to plan.

Aberdeen say their search for a replacement is underway, with their first fixture following the international break away to Kilmarnock - who are directly below them in the Premiership - on November 21.

A club statement said: "Following a board meeting, Aberdeen Football Club has today taken the decision to part company with head coach Stephen Robinson.

"Stephen leaves the club alongside assistant head coach Brian Kerr and first team coach Stephen Craigan. We thank them for their efforts during their time at Pittodrie and wish them every success for the future.

"Preparatory work to support the appointment of a new manager has been undertaken, and the recruitment process is ongoing. The focus will be on identifying the right candidate to lead the club forward and deliver the progress expected across all areas of the football operation.

"Stuart Duff will assume interim charge of first team training while the club continues its search for a new Head Coach."

"It's not worked out the way that he [Robinson] would have thought it would have.

"Coming in last year and keeping Aberdeen in the league has got to be considered a success, but obviously they lost out in the semi-final last week and it's not been the start of the season that Aberdeen would have expected.

"I've got to be honest, I think there are a lot of other factors for me why the Stephen Robertson regime at Aberdeen hasn't worked.

"There are other people in there who have got to be held accountable as well.

"It's not been great for Aberdeen. They will tell you they're the third biggest team in the country, but right now, they're miles off it and they're going to have to start getting results."

#1047. Man Utd are in relegation trouble and Carrick must be sacked

Michael Carrick stood perfectly still and raised his left arm, and his index finger, high in the air. Around him, chaos. As it had been all afternoon. Substitute Patrick Dorgu had just headed in a corner to rescue a point for Manchester United in the 96th minute and, maybe, save Carrick his job.

Going into added time and United were two goals behind. It seemed all was lost for them against Aston Villa and for their head coach, but how telling was the reaction, in the directors’ box, of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, who both jumped up in celebration? They were far more animated than Carrick and could not contain themselves.

"Football is a contact sport!" 🗣️ Did Senne Lammens foul Zion Suzuki for Man United's equaliser? 🤔 https://t.co/KCb1lHqPHP

Did their behaviour betray not just their excitement in the moment but their relief at not having to sack Carrick during this forthcoming international break? If so, they need to think again. They need to make a sober and rational decision based on evidence. And the evidence shows that Carrick must go. Because this kind of football is unsustainable. This kind of football does not work. This kind of football is stupid.

United are 18th in the Premier League. They have won one game in 10 in the league. They have conceded 15 goals in their last five matches in the league and Champions League. When they play Liverpool away, their next game, on November 22, it will be the first time they have done so from inside the relegation zone since March 1937.

They appear shockingly disorganised. Tactics seem to be an after-thought, their motivation is lacking until desperation kicks in. United conceded two goals within four minutes at the start of the game. And then two more within eight minutes of the second half kicking off.

The bottom line is this: can they afford not to make a change? If they do not, United could be accused of copping out and gambling with their status. So, Berrada and Wilcox must ask: what is Carrick doing in the dressing room and on the training ground? What messages are he and his assistant Steve Holland sending out? Are the players even listening?

At the end the fans sang Carrick’s name after United became the first team in the Premier League to come back twice from being two goals down. That also summed up the fog of confusion at a club who so obviously lack direction – from the top down – and need to get a grip of themselves. Carrick talked about having to “tighten up” the defending. But everything needs to be stronger. More taut. More competitive.

Chaos can be entertaining. Chaos can be fun. As an advert for the Premier League this was outstanding. United fans will be thrilled with the Fergie-time comeback. But chaos is also unsustainable. No one knows what to expect from United.

In the cold light of day Villa manager Unai Emery will have to ask himself whether he, too, got it wrong. His substitutions did not work, bizarrely taking off too much experience, such as his outstanding captain John McGinn, and he handed United a late initiative when it looked like all hope was lost.

But analyse the goals that United conceded. Any rational response would suggest a change should be made. Take the first two. Villa scored with their first attack, moving the ball from a throw-in, with zero pressure on them, from left to right with McGinn finding Alysson. The winger’s low first-time shot went through the legs of goalkeeper Senne Lammens, who had an awful game. Lammens’s only positive contribution was to come up for the late corner from which Dorgu scored, possibly getting away with a sly nudge on Villa’s Zion Suzuki.

What a start for Aston Villa! 🔥 Alysson fires home to give the the visitors the lead https://t.co/F0nfSRMWRa

Then Lammens conceded a second as he fumbled a shot from Alysson, after the Brazilian was again teed up by McGinn with Nicolas Jackson tucking home the rebound. It followed a poor defensive header from Leny Yoro. It would not be his last one.

Nicolas Jackson has made it 2-0 to Aston Villa after just 4 minutes and boos ring out around Old Trafford 🤯 https://t.co/G7oWDNMjGS

At that point, even so early, it felt over. For United. For Carrick. Then it got complicated. In fairness, United responded brilliantly. By half-time it was 2-2 and a potentially mutinous situation, with the fans on edge and unfurling new banners attacking the hierarchy – including one which read “your funeral not ours” – had turned and were raucous in a positive way.

Matheus Cunha, with a sharp turn and run into the Villa penalty area before being brought down, earned the spot kick from which Bruno Fernandes pulled back the first goal. Former Villa midfielder Youri Tielemans drew them level with a first-time shot. Not just that but they peppered the Villa goal.

Youri Tielemans against his former club! 😱 Manchester United are level just before the break! https://t.co/8kFOQkl814

Then they conceded two more in quick succession with a ridiculous trip on Alysson by Diogo Dalot, who was given the runaround at left-back until he was substituted to cheers. McGinn scored from the penalty. It was 4-2 when Yoro inexplicably headed a McGinn free-kick goalwards, Lammens tipped it on to the crossbar and Leon Goretzka eventually bundled the ball in.

Tellingly, the United supporters appeared too stunned to protest. The game meandered to what felt like an inevitable conclusion, petering out much like, surely, Carrick’s time in charge.

But, football, bloody hell. As someone – who was appointed United manager 40 years ago last week – once said. Dorgu made a difference. As did Joshua Zirkzee, another substitute, as the pair became United’s unlikely saviours, the striker sweeping home the full-back’s cross in the 92nd minute, with six added on.

Then a corner was won. The roar went up – as did Lammens. But it was Dorgu who met the delivery from close range to salvage a point. But the big question is: did he also salvage Carrick?

Michael Carrick has insisted he remains the right man to lead Manchester United and will not walk away despite the club being marooned in the relegation zone.

United came from 2-0 and 4-2 down to claim a last-gasp 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on another wild day at Old Trafford.It means United still only have one Premier League win to their name this season and are languishing in 18th position, a point adrift of safety, heading into the international break when the Old Trafford hierarchy must decide whether to keep faith with Carrick or appoint their third manager this year.

Carrick cut a spiky figure when asked about his future by Sky Sports and whether he would walk away.

“That’s not going to happen,” Carrick said, before asking “will there?” when it was put to him that there would “clearly” be conversations about his future.

“We haven’t won enough games, but I expect to move forward and keep working on the things we’ve been working on and showing a lot of good in the game today,” he said. “Tighten up on some things and start winning football matches.”

"That's not going to happen" 🗣️ Michael Carrick responds to the notion that he could resign as Manchester United head coach 🔴 https://t.co/q1fBKSXL7l

Asked later if he had seen enough to turn the situation around, the United head coach added: “Yeah, 100 per cent. I think there’s more than enough. Goals change games and you’ve got to deal with it, and it’s part of something we have to improve on drastically, but there’s more than enough.”Carrick scoffed at talk of United being in a relegation battle. “We’re in November,” he said. “I don’t like this situation where we are and where we’re at. But we can do something about it.”

Roy Keane, the former United captain, likened Carrick to a “politician”. “It’s hard to believe what’s coming out of the United camp because we can’t even be sure they’re being honest with themselves. It’s just words,” he said. “It’s obviously difficult for the manager. Under pressure, no doubt. He talks a lot but doesn’t say much. I don’t know if that’s a tactic. Like a politician.

“He keeps saying we need to tighten up and there’s things we need to work on. But they better get moving on that.”

Diogo Dalot’s second-half substitution was cheered by the home supporters and the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe again came under fierce attack from fans, who held up a banner in the Stretford End that read: “We don’t want a new stadium. We want new owners.” It is understood the banner was later confiscated by stewards.

Carrick defended Dalot’s contributions after another dismal showing from the Portugal defender and claimed the fans were “right behind” the players, despite growing discontent in the stands.

“I understand the frustration, I understand the disappointment of the supporters, so I get it. We’re all frustrated, we’re all disappointed,” Carrick said.

“Diogo, he gives absolutely everything. He’s played in different positions, he’s played left-back, he’s played really well at times. He gives a penalty away today, he knows that. Maybe he can do a little bit better, he’s made a mistake, but he cares an awful lot and he’s giving everything.

“I like what he brings to the team, I like what he brings to the group, I like what he brings to the whole environment and the culture that we’ve got.”

Asked if Dalot needed taking out of the team for his own good, Carrick: “Picking a team and who plays the next game, that’s a whole different decision, but it’s a whole different game that we’ve got to look forward to now.

“They [the fans] are desperate to get behind us and for us to give them something to go on and shout about. There’s frustration and disappointment at times, we all feel that. But they are right behind the boys and were at the final whistle as well.”

Unai Emery stormed straight down the tunnel before the final whistle, furious at his team’s failure to see out the game.

“We are disappointed, frustrated because in minute 90 we are winning 2-4,” the Villa manager said. “We will accept the result because we have won three and drawn three in last matches and we’re doing well. But today we have lost two points.”
